Roughly, because the original configuration has both futures, and the pivot's landing configurations inherit that variety; the desk does the inheritance honestly. Granting it: since we can steer to a nought-valent landing and also to a one-valent landing, and since steering is done one delivery at a time, somewhere there must be two configurations *one single delivery apart* — call the letter between them the switch, addressed to whomever — where landing the pivot on the earlier configuration gives nought-valence, and landing it on the later one, just one switch-delivery downstream, gives one-valence. One letter, sir — the switch — separates a nought-verdict from a one-verdict. Everything now turns on one question: at whose desk does the switch land?

Case one: the switch is addressed to someone other than Tuppy — Gussie, say. Then the pivot (to Tuppy) and the switch (to Gussie) land at different desks, and by the commuting square they commute: pivot then switch reaches exactly the same configuration as switch then pivot. Trace the two routes around the diamond. Route one: pivot lands first — the configuration is nought-valent, by hypothesis — then the switch lands. Route two: switch first, then pivot — one-valent, by hypothesis. Same final configuration, sir. And that configuration lies downstream of a nought-valent one, so every future it has ends at nought — yet route two says it is one-valent. A univalent configuration cannot re-open, and it certainly cannot be univalent in both directions at once. Contradiction. Case closed — and notice it was pure geometry: determinism and the diamond, nothing else.

Case two: the switch is addressed to Tuppy himself — the same desk as the pivot. The diamond is unavailable; deliveries to the same desk do not commute, for Tuppy reads the first letter and his state changes before the second. Here, sir, is where the argument reaches for its deepest resource — the same one the opening move used. The protocol claims to tolerate a crash. Tuppy's crash, in particular. So: from the earlier of our two configurations, freeze Tuppy — the scheduler simply declines, lawfully for any finite stretch, to give him a turn or a letter — and let Bingo and Gussie play on alone. Must they reach a verdict? They must. If Tuppy had genuinely crashed, termination obliges the survivors to finish; and — the doppelgänger, third appearance tonight — Bingo and Gussie cannot tell a crashed Tuppy from a benched one. The letters in the bag addressed to Tuppy sit undelivered either way; his silence is identical silence in both worlds. Whatever the survivors would do with Tuppy dead, they must do with Tuppy benched, for the two worlds are one world to them. So they play to a verdict; ink dries; call the resulting configuration the verdict configuration.

And now the trap closes — watch the diamond return with a vengeance. The survivors' entire play touched neither the pivot nor the switch: both are letters addressed to Tuppy, and Tuppy was benched throughout. So their play commutes with each of them — the commuting square again, iterated. From the verdict configuration, let the scheduler now deliver the pivot: by commutation, the result is the same as if the pivot had landed *first*, back at the start, followed by the survivors' play — and the pivot landing there, you will recall, gave nought-valence; so the verdict configuration has a future ending in nought. Alternatively, from the verdict configuration, deliver the switch and then the pivot: commuting both across the survivors' play, this is switch-then-pivot back at the start — the landing we said gives one-valence — followed by their play, and so a future ending in one. Both futures, alive, at the verdict configuration. The verdict configuration is bivalent — on the fence. But ink is dry at the verdict configuration, sir — and we established, as the bolt fastening this whole proof, that ink implies univalence. A configuration cannot be both inked and bivalent. Contradiction — final, and fatal. The supposition falls; the pivot lemma stands. From the fence, any owed letter can be paid and the fence held.

**The endgame.** Fourth movement, and it is short, because the war is won and this is the occupation. The scheduler's full campaign, assembled: open at a bivalent configuration — initial bivalence guarantees one exists. Now run the parliament on a rota: Bingo, Tuppy, Gussie, Bingo, Tuppy, Gussie, round and round, forever. On each gentleman's turn, take the *oldest* letter owed him in the bag — oldest first, so nothing lingers — declare it the pivot, and play the pivot lemma: steer, deliver it, land on the fence. Then the next gentleman, his oldest letter, the fence again. Audit the leash, sir, strap by strap. Every gentleman receives turns forever — the rota sees to it. Every letter is eventually delivered — it waits at most one circuit of the rota before becoming somebody's oldest, and then the lemma lands it. The run is fair. It is fairness itself. Nobody has crashed — the dark privilege, note it well, was never exercised; every gentleman is alive, industrious, corresponding at full diligence from the first move to the — but there is no last move. The game continues forever, every configuration along it bivalent, and a bivalent configuration has clean books. No gentleman ever inks. Termination fails in a fair, crash-free, loss-free execution — and the protocol, which promised termination in *every* fair execution, is refuted. No protocol survives. That is the theorem, sir. That is FLP entire.

Let us stand in the ruins for a moment, as we did on the hill with the generals, because this proof has a property I want you to carry out of the room. Ask: what did the adversary actually *do*? It lost nothing — every letter arrived. It forged nothing, duplicated nothing. It crashed no one — the dark privilege stayed sheathed, start to finish. Its entire output, over an infinite game, was a sequence of perfectly legal decisions about *when* — this letter now, that gentleman next. And yet it was the crash that did the killing. Not a crash that happened: the crash that *might*. Twice in the proof — at the opening, and in the heart's second case — the argument reached for the same lever: the protocol is required to survive a silent chair, therefore the survivors must be prepared to finish without any given colleague, therefore the scheduler can bench that colleague and *borrow* the survivors' preparedness — march them down the very corridor built for the emergency, then produce the missing man alive and use the corridor's existence to spring the trap. The tolerance is the vulnerability. The fire escape is how the burglar gets in. Every fault-tolerant protocol must be willing to proceed on silence, and everything that proceeds on silence can be led by silence — hesitation, sir, wielded as a weapon; the threat sufficing where the deed is never done. I permit myself the episode's one open admiration here, as budgeted, because I know of nothing else in computing quite like this argument: three pages that took the field's fondest ambition, granted it every concession it had ever asked of the network — every letter delivered, every process scheduled — and defeated it with the one thing no message-passing system can buy at any price: an answer to the question *is he dead, or merely slow?* The confusion we filed in episode one as the primordial nuisance turns out to be a conservation law. The corner the decade of tinkerers kept moving was this corner. It cannot close, because it is load-bearing.

### Part Four — The Fine Print

An impossibility theorem misremembered is worse than none — episode one's rule — and this theorem is misremembered for a living. So, the fine print, read aloud, clause by clause.

What exactly was proven? In the asynchronous model — no bounds on delay, none on relative speed — no *deterministic* protocol can *guarantee* agreement, validity, and *termination* for even a single bit, in every fair execution, while tolerating even one crash-stop failure. Each italicized word is load-bearing, and each is a hinge on which the escape gates of part five will turn.

First: termination is the casualty — the only casualty. Nothing in the proof touches agreement or validity; indeed the constructed run never violates them — it never lets anyone decide at all. The field has a pair of words for the two sides of that asymmetry, and I want them in your vocabulary before we go a step further, because you will meet them unglossed in every paper you read hereafter. Agreement and validity are *safety* properties: the promise that nothing bad ever happens — no two verdicts differ, no verdict is conjured from nowhere. Termination is a *liveness* property: the promise that something good eventually does happen — the meeting ends. And the asymmetry between the two is the single most practical sentence tonight, so let me give it the whiteboard phrasing now: safety is free; liveness is the hostage. There exist protocols — you operate several — that never, in any execution, under any weather, ink two different verdicts: safety unconditional, held through arbitrary asynchrony, through crashes, through the scheduler's worst. What no protocol can do is *also* promise the meeting always ends. The parliament that cannot be made to lie can still be made to filibuster. When we meet Paxos next week you will see this division of the estate made explicit in the protocol's very structure: its safety argument will invoke no clocks, no timeouts, no luck — and its liveness section will begin, in effect, "assuming the weather improves." That sentence is not an engineering apology, sir. It is FLP, cited as fine print.

Second: deterministic. The scheduler's campaign was a tablebase strategy — it steered toward the fence because, holding the rulebook, it could compute where the fence was. Every reaction predictable, every fence position calculable. Put a coin in any gentleman's pocket — let his rulebook say, in some corner, "flip" — and the tablebase clouds over: configurations no longer have a determinate valence, the fence is no longer a computable line, and the whole campaign wants re-litigating. That is not yet a solution — it is a doorway, and Ben-Or is standing in it; part five.

Third: one faulty process. The title's modesty, and its menace. The theorem does not require an elaborate failure model — no lying, no forging, no Byzantine aunts; one possible crash-stop, the gentlest failure in the taxonomy, suffices to poison the well. And mind the grammar of "possible": in the killing run itself, nobody crashes. It is the protocol's obligation to *survive* a crash — the fire escape it is required to build — that the adversary turns. A protocol for machines guaranteed immortal escapes the theorem trivially; a protocol for the actual world, where the guarantee cannot be had, walks into it.

Fourth: the reformed Post. Say it once more, because it is the detail the folklore always drops: no loss. Two Generals was an impossibility of *loss* — kill a letter and knowledge cannot become common. FLP is an impossibility of *delay* — deliver every letter, and mere freedom about when still forbids guaranteed agreement. They are different theorems about different liberties of the Post, and the pairing brackets the field's misery from both ends: the network that loses defeats certainty of knowledge; the network that dawdles defeats certainty of termination. An engineer who remembers only "networks are unreliable" has learned half the lesson. The reliable network with no latency bound is *also* a theorem-grade adversary.

Now the other side of the ledger — what was *not* proven, because the folklore here is a standing hazard to good engineering. The theorem does not say consensus is impossible in practice. It does not say your etcd cluster is broken, or that its designers evaded mathematics by marketing. The killing schedule is a single infinite thread through the tree of executions, woven with tablebase precision; disturb it at any of infinitely many points — one letter landing a moment early, one timeout misfiring in our favour — and the parliament falls off the fence and decides. Real networks, whose delays are noisy rather than malicious, wander off the razor's edge almost immediately, which is why your clusters decide millions of times a day and why the theorem's shadow in production is not deadlock but the rarer, stranger thing: the election storm — leadership contested, contested again, term after term climbing while no term completes — livelock, the fence walked in the wild, always briefly, under weather that merely *resembles* the adversary for a while. FLP does not predict routine failure. It forbids a certain sentence from ever being true: "this system is *guaranteed* to decide, whatever the timing." Any vendor page containing that sentence about an asynchronous deterministic system is selling you a theorem violation, and you are entitled — episode one's triage — to ask which word they are quietly redefining: the model, the guarantee, or the price.

### Part Five — The Loopholes

A good impossibility theorem, sir, is not a wall but a survey: it tells you precisely where the fence runs, and therefore precisely where the gates must be. The italicized words of part four were the survey markers — asynchronous, deterministic, guarantee. Three words, three gates, and the entire practising industry files through them daily. Let us tour all three, because episode after episode from here forward will be spent on the far side of one or another, and I want the gate stamped in your passport each time we cross.

Gate one: renegotiate *asynchronous* — partial synchrony. The fence was surveyed in the model where delay is boundless and the scheduler's aim eternal. But recall episode one's middle terrain, the one I asked you to mark well: partial synchrony, articulated by Cynthia Dwork, Nancy Lynch — the same Lynch, sir, fencing from both sides, having proven the impossibility she now helps to escape — and Larry Stockmeyer, in a paper published in nineteen eighty-eight in the Journal of the ACM under the title "Consensus in the Presence of Partial Synchrony." Its two readings you know: bounds exist but are unknown; or bounds hold only after some unknown stabilization time. Its consensus finding is the industry's charter: in partial synchrony, consensus is solvable — with safety holding *unconditionally*, through the wild weather, and termination guaranteed *once the weather settles*. Note the shape, because it is the only shape the mathematics permits: not "the protocol terminates," but "the protocol never errs, and terminates when the network behaves for long enough." The guarantee is conditional exactly where FLP says it must be, and unconditional exactly where safety is free. Every timeout in every consensus deployment you operate is this gate in miniature — a wager that the bound, whatever it is, has probably been reached; every adaptive timeout, doubling patiently, is a protocol groping for the unknown bound from below. The industry does not defeat FLP, sir. It rents a better model by the millisecond and keeps the receipts. Episode four lives entirely inside this gate, and I shall say no more tonight.

Gate two: renegotiate *deterministic* — randomization. Nineteen eighty-three, a year before the partial-synchrony paper's conference debut and the same year FLP itself was first presented: Michael Ben-Or, in a conference paper of a handful of pages — this field's monuments are short, sir; suspect the long ones — titled "Another Advantage of Free Choice." The advantage in question: a coin the scheduler cannot read. Ben-Or's protocol proceeds in rounds of votes; when a round's votes are decisive, gentlemen adopt and eventually ink; when they are not, each gentleman flips his private coin for a fresh opinion and tries again. The scheduler still controls all timing — but the fence campaign required *steering*, and steering requires forecasting reactions, and a coin has no forecast. The tablebase is blind one move ahead, forever. The price of the gate is stated with equal honesty: termination is guaranteed only *with probability one* — certainty of a new and weaker currency; the meeting ends almost surely, but no fixed deadline can be promised, and with naive private coins the expected wait grows savage as the parliament grows — exponential rounds in the worst arrangements. There are repairs — coins shared among the company, cryptographic and otherwise, bring the expectation down to civilized figures — and the whole trade-off is a starred door at tonight's desk, where a guided problem walks you through Ben-Or's safety and his lovely termination argument: with probability one, some round's coins all land the same way, and unanimity, once achieved, is never surrendered. The gate is real, it is beautiful, and the industry uses it less than the theory admires it — mostly because gate one is cheaper and the tooling won. But mark it as the answer to a precise question: it is the *deterministic* in FLP doing exact work.

Gate three: renegotiate the interface — failure detectors. This gate is subtler and, for your trade, the most clarifying. Nineteen ninety-six, Journal of the ACM, Tushar Chandra and Sam Toueg: instead of changing the timing model wholesale, package the timing assumption behind an interface. Give each gentleman one additional instrument, and it carries the name the literature prints on it: a *failure detector* — a suspicion service at his elbow, a little oracle maintaining a list of colleagues it currently suspects of being dead. The detector may be wrong, sir — that is the entire point. It may slander the living; it may, for a while, acquit the dead; it may change its mind hourly. Chandra and Toueg's question: how much *eventual* honesty must such a failure detector deliver for consensus to become solvable? Their celebrated answer — one of a family, and the family's weakest useful member: it suffices that *eventually, some one correct gentleman is never again suspected by any survivor* — that, plus a majority of the parliament alive, and consensus is solvable. All the slander in the world, forgiven, so long as the detector eventually settles on trusting somebody trustworthy. And the companion result — Chandra with Vassos Hadzilacos and Toueg, same journal, same year — closed the question from below: the *weakest* failure detector that suffices is exactly an eventual-leader service, one that eventually points every survivor at the same living gentleman. That one has a name of a single letter, and you should carry it out of the room: the field calls it *Omega*, and writes it as the Greek capital of that name. The weakest failure detector for consensus is Omega — a sentence you will meet unglossed, and now need no gloss for. I state the theorem with respect and decline its proof, which is genuinely beyond this course — the honesty clause, exercised. But do not let the abstraction fool you into thinking this gate theoretical: a suspicion service is a *timeout with its epistemology showing*. Every health check in your fleet, every phi-accrual dial, every lease expiry is an implementation of an unreliable failure detector; the theory's contribution is the specification — how little accuracy suffices, and what the protocol may lawfully do with slanderous evidence. The instalments arrive on schedule: episode five arms the detectors with leases and fences; episode eleven prices their false positives in retry storms.

Three gates, sir, and one observation to bind them, worth a pin through the whole part: all three purchase the same commodity by different contracts. Partial synchrony buys it with time — eventually the network calms and a leader's authority sticks. Randomization buys it with luck — eventually the coins align. Failure detectors buy it with delegated suspicion — eventually the oracle settles on a leader all can follow. In each case the purchased good is a *stretch of settled asymmetry*: some interval in which one distinguished gentleman is, and is believed to be, in charge for long enough to shepherd a decision through. That is the commodity FLP proves cannot be manufactured from asynchronous determinism alone — and next week, when the Synod of a vanished Greek island convenes, you will watch a protocol whose safety needs no such commodity at all, and whose liveness is precisely the art of acquiring it gracefully.

### Part Six — One Bad Afternoon

We change theorems now, though not, you will notice, technique. From the profound impossibility to the famous one: from the theorem every engineer should know and few can state, to the theorem every engineer can state and few state correctly. It concerns not eternity but one bad afternoon, and it will take us two minutes to prove and rather longer to disinfect.

The history, dates exact. In July of the year two thousand, at the ACM's Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing — the field's own parliament — Eric Brewer of Berkeley delivered an invited keynote proposing a rule of thumb from a decade of building web systems: of three desirable properties — consistency, availability, and tolerance of network partitions — a system may have at most two. A conjecture, offered as engineering folk-wisdom in the honourable sense. Two years later, in two thousand two, Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch — the same Nancy Lynch a third time tonight, sir; the woman fences on every piste in this field — published a short formalization and proof in SIGACT News, and the conjecture became the CAP theorem: Brewer's initials-friendly christening, Gilbert and Lynch's mathematics.

But a theorem is its definitions, so we take the three letters slowly, each with its exact meaning, because every abuse of this result begins with a blurred letter.

C, consistency, means here something quite specific: linearizability. We devote episode seven to that word — it is a debt formally issued tonight — and until then, the honest informal reading: the replicated service behaves, observably, as if there were a single copy of the data, applying operations one at a time, respecting real time — every read returns the latest completed write, full stop. Not "consistent" as your transactions department uses it, not "the data satisfies my invariants," not eventual anything. One-copy behaviour, sir. The strictest promise on the shelf, wearing the field's most abused word.

A, availability, means: every request that arrives at any non-failed node eventually receives a meaningful response. Attend to the quantifier — *every* request, at *every* surviving node. Not "the service stays up for most clients," not "the majority side keeps answering." If one lonely node on the wrong side of a partition receives a read and cannot answer it, availability — in the theorem's exacting sense — is forfeit. The theorem's A is total; the marketing department's A is a fraction with some nines in it; the two share a letter and nothing else.

P, partition tolerance, means: the guarantee in question survives the Post severing itself — provinces of the network isolated, every letter between them lost, for as long as the outage lasts. And here mark the asymmetry that undoes most recitations of this theorem: C and A are goods you promise; P is weather. Episode one entered the documentary record — the Bailis and Kingsbury catalogue, the correlated redundancy, the sharks; partitions are not a menu item you decline, they are a thing the world does to you. "Choosing" partition intolerance is choosing to have no promise for one of the afternoons that will certainly come.

The theorem: in an asynchronous network subject to partitions, no read-write storage service provides both linearizability and total availability. Two out of the trio, with P not optional. And now the proof, aloud and entire, as budgeted at two minutes — after FLP it will feel like a stroll, and the punchline is an old friend.

Sever the shop. Bingo's branch in one province; Gussie's in the other; the Post between them dead for the afternoon — every letter across the divide, lost. Both gentlemen are healthy, their provinces internally sound. Now, Bertie — forever a client, forever inconveniently timed — conducts two items of business. First: he writes to Bingo's side — update the delivery address, from the old to the new. Bingo is a non-failed node holding a request; availability compels a meaningful response; the write completes, acknowledged, on Bingo's side of the silence. Second: Bertie — or his man of business, or any client anywhere; the theorem needs only one reader — reads the delivery address from Gussie's side. Gussie is a non-failed node holding a request; availability compels an answer. And now the doppelgänger, fourth and final appearance tonight, performing the two-minute version of the murder: what does Gussie's province know of Bertie's write? Nothing. No letter crossed; none will while the afternoon lasts. To every gentleman in Gussie's province, this world — write executed beyond the divide — is indistinguishable from the world in which no write ever happened. Identical observations compel identical behaviour: whatever Gussie would answer in the writeless world, he must answer in this one. In the writeless world he answers the old address — it is the only address his province has ever contained. So he answers the old address here: a completed write, invisible to a subsequent read. Linearizability — one-copy behaviour, latest write — is violated, publicly, in a two-line trace. The only escape: let Gussie *not* answer — refuse, or stall until the Post heals. And that surrenders availability, total as the theorem demands it. Choose your betrayal, sir. On the partitioned afternoon, C and A cannot both be kept, and no ingenuity is pending that changes it, for the proof used nothing but the fact that information cannot cross a silence. That is the CAP theorem — Gilbert and Lynch dressed it in registers and formality, and the desk tonight reproduces their rigour, including their further result for partially synchronous timing, which survives the trip intact. The mathematics is honestly this small. It fit in a keynote slide in two thousand; it fits in two minutes tonight.

Which makes the subsequent decade of abuse all the more instructive, and I shall now prosecute the folklore with the relish promised in episode one, where I declared — you may recall the phrasing — that most citations of a certain three-letter theorem in vendor keynotes are theorems quoted shorn of their models, like maritime law cited in a desert. Exhibit by exhibit.

Abuse the first: "choose two of three," recited as if C, A, and P were three dishes and every architect picks a pair. You now know better twice over. P is weather — it is not chosen, it arrives; a "CA system" is a system with no stated behaviour for an afternoon that is certainly coming, which is not a category but a confession, an unstated model in the sense of episode one's discipline. And in fair weather — no partition in progress — the theorem is silent entirely: nothing in Gilbert and Lynch prevents a well-built system from being consistent *and* available on every ordinary day, and the good ones are. The honest sentence is smaller and sharper: *when* a partition strikes, and only then, each affected operation must betray either consistency or availability. The theorem is a theorem about one bad afternoon. Its citation as a universal design trilemma is heraldry, not law.

Abuse the second: the labels. An industry of taxonomists arose, stamping each database CP or AP, as though the theorem issued licence plates. Mr. Kleppmann — our standing companion's author — published in two thousand fifteen a critique, and a plea whose title-sentiment I endorse and assign tonight: please stop calling databases CP or AP. The letters, remember, are extremes: C is full linearizability, A is every-node-answers. Real systems are neither pole: they are configurable per operation, quorum-tunable, differently-behaved for reads and writes; a system may serve linearizable writes and stale-tolerant reads in the same breath, and most do — the label compresses a contract worth reading into a syllable worth nothing. When a vendor page says "CP," sir, the diligent question is episode one's question: which failures, which guarantee, at which price — show me the afternoon in the documentation.

Abuse the third, subtler, and the one whose correction earns its keep in design reviews: treating the partition dichotomy as binary when it is a dial. Nineteen ninety-nine, before the conjecture was even conjectured publicly: Armando Fox and the same Brewer published "Harvest, Yield, and Scalable Tolerant Systems," which offers the grown-up vocabulary for degradation. Yield: the fraction of requests answered. Harvest: the fraction of the relevant data each answer reflects. The partitioned search service that answers every query from the reachable half of its index has kept its yield and halved its harvest — every client served, every answer honest about being partial. The banking service that refuses writes on the minority side has spent yield to keep harvest whole. Between "consistent" and "available" there runs a whole negotiated frontier — answer with a bound on staleness, answer with an explicit partial-results flag, accept writes locally with declared reconciliation debts, the shopping cart's whole future lives out here — and systems that degrade *well* are precisely systems whose designers chose a point on the frontier deliberately, in peacetime, and wrote it down. CAP names the frontier's endpoints. Harvest and yield survey the middle, where the actual engineering lives.

And abuse the fourth — the omission, the one that costs the most money: partition-fixation. The CAP framing lets the unwary conclude that consistency's price is paid only on the bad afternoon, so a sturdy network makes strong consistency free. It does not, and the corrective is the grown-up formulation the plan promised: PACELC, proposed by Daniel Abadi of Yale in a column in IEEE Computer in two thousand twelve. The scheme reads: if Partition, then the trade is Availability versus Consistency — CAP, conceded; Else — in ordinary weather, which is most weather — the trade is Latency versus Consistency. For consider what one-copy behaviour costs on a perfectly healthy network: coordination. The write that must be seen by every subsequent read everywhere must reach agreement machinery — a quorum's round trip, a leader's confirmation — before acknowledgment; the toll is collected on *every* write, on the *best* afternoon, and it is collected in the currency your users actually feel. Latency collects even in peacetime, sir — that is PACELC's sentence, and it explains at a stroke the entire respectable half of the eventual-consistency industry: geo-replicated systems relax consistency not mainly because partitions terrify them but because the speed of light bills them daily; episode one priced Toronto to Sydney at a sixth of a second, and no theorem is required to find that expensive, merely a profit-and-loss statement. You will, before the season is out, see the invoice paid in the other direction — a company purchasing consistency across continents by buying better physics, seven milliseconds of deliberate waiting at a time. Both sides of that ledger are PACELC's E-clause in action. CAP is the afternoon the network betrays you. PACELC is every day, including that one.

There. The famous theorem, proven and disinfected. Two minutes of mathematics, ten years of misquotation, one afternoon of weather — and one more entry for a pattern you should now be noticing: the doppelgänger felled consensus in the grand theorem and felled the two-out-of-three dream in the small one, with the identical thrust — two worlds, one observer, no telling them apart. The master key, as advertised. By episode eight, when it walks in wearing a notary's collar to convict two-phase commit, I expect you to hear the footsteps in the first paragraph.

### Part Seven — The Triage

Two theorems tonight, of very different weights, both routinely miscited — which makes tonight the correct evening to install, as promised in episode one, the course's standing triage. When any claim of the form "that cannot be done" crosses your desk — in a design review, a vendor negotiation, a postmortem, an architecture council — it goes into one of three bins, and the sorting is, I would submit, the most consequential single habit this course will leave you with.

Bin one: impossible. A theorem applies — this model, this guarantee, this exact ask — and the answer is no, permanently, for everyone, including the vendor whose deck says otherwise. Guaranteed-terminating deterministic consensus in pure asynchrony with a possible crash: bin one, by FLP. Linearizability with every-node availability through a partition: bin one, by Gilbert and Lynch. Certainty of common action over a channel that may lose the last letter: bin one, by the generals. The correct response to bin one is never effort; it is renegotiation — change the model (buy synchrony, buy detectors), change the guarantee (probability one, eventual, bounded-stale), or change the ask. The bin's discipline cuts both ways, mind: to *place* a claim here you must produce the theorem and match its model to your world, clause by clause — episode one's rule that a theorem quoted without its model is a noise. Most things called impossible in industry are not in this bin. Which brings us to —

Bin two: expensive. Possible, proven so, shipping in production — and carrying a price tag that arrives on schedule, forever. Consensus under partial synchrony: possible, at the price of timeout tuning, election storms in bad weather, and a liveness clause that reads "when the network settles." Linearizability across a continent: possible, at a round trip — or at seven milliseconds of purchased physics — per write, every write, peacetime included; PACELC's E-clause is bin two's ledger. Exactly-once *effect*: possible — episode ten — at the price of idempotence engineering throughout. The correct response to bin two is neither refusal nor heroism; it is an invoice: name the recurring cost, decide who pays it, and write both down. Most of the season from episode four onward, sir, is a walking tour of bin two — the honest accounting of how the impossible's neighbours are made routine, at what price, in which model.

Bin three: merely inadvisable. Possible, affordable — and unwise, for your workload, this year. Consensus on the critical path of every read when a lease would do. Strong consistency for a cache whose staleness nobody can observe. A cross-region transaction where a schema change would dissolve the need — we shall make that one a proverb in due course. Bin three is the bin of judgment, and it has a diagnostic all its own: bins one and two are properties of mathematics and markets, but bin three is a property of *your* requirements, and it is the only bin whose contents change when the business does. The senior failure mode is misfiling between two and three — paying bin-two invoices out of habit for guarantees the product stopped needing, or declaring bin-three inconveniences "impossible" to end a meeting. You have seen both, sir. So have I, and I was not always the one who caught it.

Impossible, expensive, merely inadvisable. When the claim crosses your desk: which bin, on whose theorem or whose invoice or whose judgment — and the conversation that follows is, in my experience, shorter and considerably more honest than the one it replaces.

### Closing — The Whiteboard and the Ledger

The Whiteboard, then. Four items, for the designer walking into a review.

Item one. State the model before citing the impossibility — either impossibility, any impossibility. FLP names its terms: asynchronous, deterministic, one crash tolerated, guaranteed termination. CAP names its terms: a partition in progress, total availability, linearizability. Quote the theorem with its terms attached or not at all; a three-letter incantation without its model is heraldry, and design reviews are not the College of Arms.

Item two. Safety is free; liveness is the hostage. FLP forbids guarantees of termination — it does not forbid success, and it never touches correctness. So interrogate any consensus-bearing design at exactly the joint the theorem names: what does this system do while it cannot decide? What do clients see during the election storm, and what is the story when the storm outlives the deadline? A design with a crisp answer has read its FLP; a design that answers "that won't happen" has not, and the scheduler is patient.

Item three. CAP is a theorem about one bad afternoon; PACELC is about every day. Budget both, separately, in writing: the partition posture — which operations betray consistency and which betray availability when the Post severs, chosen in peacetime, tested on schedule — and the peacetime toll — what every write pays for the consistency level you have selected, in milliseconds, on the invoice where the users can feel it. A review that discusses only the afternoon has priced the flood and forgotten the rent. And between the poles, remember the dials with names: harvest and yield — degrade deliberately, not accidentally.

Item four. Triage every impossibility claim into its bin — impossible, expensive, merely inadvisable — and demand the paperwork appropriate to the bin: a theorem with matching model for the first; a recurring invoice with a named payer for the second; a requirements argument, dated this fiscal year, for the third.

The reading, three pieces, all short — this field's monuments are short.

First, the text itself: Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson, "Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process," Journal of the ACM, April nineteen eighty-five. I assign it whole, and I assign the *experience* of it as much as the content: put an evening aside expecting a fortress and find nine pages, of which the fatal argument is three. Read their third lemma twice — it is tonight's pivot lemma, the fence held with the pen of a working mathematician, and the compression I performed aloud is redeemed there in full. When you finish, look up from the page and recall that this fenced off a corner of the possible for every machine that will ever be built. Three pages, sir.

Second: Gilbert and Lynch, "Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services," SIGACT News, two thousand two. Equally short. Read it for the definitions above all — what "available" totally means, what "consistent" precisely is — and note their second theorem, the partially-synchronous variant, which the keynotes never mention. And after it, as disinfectant, Mr. Kleppmann's critique from two thousand fifteen — the plea about the licence plates.

Third: Abadi's PACELC column, IEEE Computer, two thousand twelve. One evening, one acronym more euphonious than most, and a permanent upgrade to your vocabulary for exactly the conversation item three demands.

The desk now awaits with chapter three, and tonight it is the volume's flagship, stated as such with relish. The consensus problem formal; the game, the configurations, the valence apparatus; the commuting square as a lemma with last week's fingerprints on it; the pivot lemma with the compressed case written out to the last inequality — my debt from the set piece, redeemed in full; the endgame construction with its fairness audit; and the whole assembled as the Fischer–Lynch–Paterson theorem, entire, the proof this volume was built to hold. Gilbert and Lynch formalized alongside, both timing models. The problems in three tiers, as framed tonight: valence drills on a toy parliament small enough to see whole; the harvest-and-yield vocabulary made formal; the distinction between agreement among survivors and agreement binding even the dead — uniform agreement, a subtlety with a body count; and a sabotage problem I commend to you with particular warmth — the impatient tribunal, a rotating-chairman protocol of entirely plausible construction, the kind of thing a strong engineer designs on a Tuesday whiteboard, whose timeout-based suspicions can be arranged, by a scheduler of tonight's calibre, into two chairmen inking two different verdicts in the same afternoon. Per the standing rules: I certify the bug fatal; the split-brain execution is written out in the solutions, ink and all. Two starred doors for the ambitious: Ben-Or's coin walked through with a guide — safety, validity, and the lovely almost-sure termination argument — and the reduction that drags atomic broadcast into FLP's grave with consensus, so you may see how an impossibility, once proven for the atom, propagates up the periodic table.

And the ledger. An instalment falls due tonight, and I am pleased to pay it before the audience: crashed-versus-slow, issued in episode one — managed, never cured — tonight received its formal apparatus: the confusion was commissioned as the scheduler, and then promoted to murder weapon — the proof of the season's flagship theorem turns, at both of its critical junctures, on precisely the two worlds no survivor can tell apart. The debt is not retired, sir — it cannot be retired; that is rather the theorem — but it is now managed by mathematics instead of by anecdote, with further instalments to come. Three fresh debts issued tonight: partial synchrony, surveyed as gate one, is cashed next week, when protocols move in and furnish it; the failure detectors of gate three await their machinery and their price; and the C of CAP — linearizability, tonight defined by gesture and promissory note — will in due course receive its full legal definition, when the most overloaded word in computing is finally read its rights.

Next week, then: the parliament of our title. In nineteen ninety, Leslie Lamport — the third time the portrait has presided over an episode, and not the last — submits to the field a paper describing the fault-tolerant legislature of a vanished Greek island called Paxos, its protocol reconstructed from archaeological fragments, its correctness argued in the voice of an amateur classicist. The reviewers request the removal of the jokes. The author declines. The paper enters a drawer, and remains there for eight years, while the industry outside the drawer builds, badly, the very thing inside it — published at last in nineteen ninety-eight, by which time the field had learned to need it. My sympathies in the affair, sir, are theatrically divided, and I shall itemize them at the proper moment. We will not recite the protocol; recitation is how Paxos acquired its reputation. We will *derive* it — begin with naive majority voting, watch it deadlock, repair it, watch the repair lose a chosen value, repair the repair — every rule a scar with a story, until the Synod stands before you as the only shape it could ever have taken, and the fence of tonight is escaped through gate one with the toll paid in full view. The doppelgänger may take a well-earned week in the stalls. The crowded-club lemma makes its debut on the boards.

Until then, sir.

*— End of Episode Three.*

## Episode 4 — The Part-Time Parliament

*An Audio Course in Distributed Systems — Episode Four: The Part-Time Parliament*

### The Island in the Drawer

Good day, sir.

In nineteen ninety, Leslie Lamport — whose portrait has now presided over three of our four evenings, a frequency I promise reflects the field's architecture rather than my own devotion — submitted to the ACM's Transactions on Computer Systems a paper describing the parliament of a vanished Greek island called Paxos. The Paxons, the paper explained, had solved a delicate problem: their legislators were part-time — merchants and mariners, forever wandering out of the chamber on business, returning hours or days later — their messengers were unreliable, and yet the island's laws had to remain consistent: one law per numbered slot in the ledgers, the same law in every legislator's copy, no matter who wandered where. The paper reconstructed their protocol from archaeological fragments, complete with the names of Paxon dignitaries rendered in a phonetic Greek that, on inspection, encoded the names of contemporary computer scientists, and its correctness argument was conducted in the voice of an amateur classicist reporting the findings of one Παρλιαμεντ — forgive me, sir; the temptation passes.

The reviewers were not amused. More precisely — and the distinction matters to the story — they found the result interesting and the presentation insufferable, and they requested, in the way reviewers do, that the Indiana-Jones business be removed and the theorems be left to stand in decent academic dress. The author's position was that the jokes were load-bearing. Neither side yielded. And so a paper containing the solution to fault-tolerant consensus — the working, practical escape through the very gate our previous evening surveyed — went into a drawer, and stayed there for eight years, while outside the drawer the industry shipped lock managers and replication schemes and failover scripts that reinvented fragments of its contents, usually wrongly, at considerable expense. It was published at last in nineteen ninety-eight, jokes intact, by which time the field had learned enough to need it desperately and to forgive it almost anything.

My sympathies in the affair, sir, are theatrically divided, and since I promised you an itemization: as a professional with standards regarding prose, I hold that a correctness argument owes its reader every courtesy, and burying the decade's most important protocol under a fictional archaeology was, let us say, an aggressive courtesy. As a gentleman's gentleman, however, I observe that the reviewers were offered the answer to their field's central question and declined it over a matter of costume — a parable on the perils of wit among the humourless, and I confess I take the author's side with more feeling than is strictly professional. The field has since split the difference in its habitual manner: it kept the result, discarded the island, and named everything after it anyway. Our course borrowed the paper's spirit for its very title — this is the debt I promised in the founding session to explain, and it stands explained: a parliament of machines, part-time, unreliable, and lawful nonetheless.

Tonight, then: consensus achieved. Last week mathematics forbade it — in the asynchronous model, deterministically, with certainty of termination. Tonight we walk through gate one, partial synchrony, and build the thing that lives on the far side. And I must tell you how the building will proceed, because the method is the moral. I shall not recite Paxos at you. Recitation is how Paxos acquired its reputation as incomprehensible — a liturgy of prepares and promises that seem arbitrary until one has personally needed each of them. We shall instead *derive* it: begin with the naive protocol every competent engineer would sketch on a Tuesday, watch it die, repair it, watch the repair die more subtly, and repair again — twice — until the Synod of Paxos stands before you as the only shape it could ever have taken. Every rule a scar, sir, and every scar with a story. Then the fine print the theorem of last week demands; then Raft, the humane modern re-tailoring, with its famous trap staged in full; then a paragraph of overdue justice for an unsung ancestor; and at the last, a theorem of Mr. Herlihy's that explains why this one small agreement is the atom from which everything else in the season will be built.

### Part One — One Law at a Time

Size the problem honestly before solving it, because half of Paxos's reputation for difficulty is the difficulty of three problems being solved at once by people who thought they were solving one. Tonight, the single-decree problem — one law, decided once — and nothing else. The log of many laws is next week's business; elections and thrones will enter tonight only as liveness machinery, exactly as last week's theorem said they must.

The setting, with the company in their accustomed places. The umbrella shop must fix a single by-law — say, whether Thursday deliveries shall be free. Motions may originate anywhere: Bingo may move one version, Tuppy another; Bertie, as ever, merely wants to know what was decided, preferably before Thursday. The gentlemen who hold copies and cast votes — *acceptors*, in the field's word and therefore in ours; the parliament, when we speak of them as a body — are our three: Bingo, Tuppy, and Gussie, each keeping his own ledger. The Post is its usual self: delays without bound, but tonight, as last night, no forgery and no permanent loss. And the failure model, mark it: gentlemen may crash — and may also *recover*, wandering back into the chamber with whatever their written ledger preserved. Part-time legislators, sir, in the paper's exact spirit. Which imposes the rule I shall call amnesia forbidden: anything a gentleman must stand behind later, he writes in the ledger before answering — because a promise remembered only in one's head does not survive a nap, and a parliament of nappers that forgets its promises will, as the desk will demonstrate with a certified disaster, cheerfully vote both sides of the same question.

A word on offices before we legislate, because the paper's division of labour confuses newcomers into imagining three kinds of machine. There are three *roles*, sir, not three species. A **proposer** is whoever currently has ambitions for the by-law: tonight, Bingo and Tuppy both, which is precisely the trouble. An **acceptor** is a keeper of the ledger and a caster of votes — the parliament proper, and the only office whose conduct decides safety. A **learner** is anyone who wishes to discover what was chosen without necessarily having voted — Bertie's whole existence, this week. One machine ordinarily holds all three commissions at once, the way a gentleman may be simultaneously a voter, a candidate, and a reader of newspapers. Keep the offices separate in your head all the same: every rule tonight belongs to exactly one of them, and half the folklore confusion about Paxos comes from asking why a voter is doing a candidate's paperwork.

And a word on arithmetic, because "majority" was chosen over its rivals for reasons worth having explicitly. Why not require *unanimity* — every gentleman accepts, no doubts anywhere? Because unanimity tolerates no absentees: one gentleman in the bath and the house is struck dumb, which surrenders the entire fault-tolerance ambition that brought us here — we distribute, you will recall, *because* machines fail. Why not a *fixed pair* — say, Bingo and Tuppy constitute a quorum by appointment? Because the appointment concentrates the fragility: lose one appointee and no quorum can ever form again. The majority is the arrangement that spreads the risk evenly and prices it honestly: a parliament of three proceeds despite any one absentee; a parliament of five despite any two; in general the house survives the silence of just under half its members — and this, sir, is the exact exchange rate between seats purchased and failures survived, the first line of a cost table we shall extend across the season. The deeper truth — and the reason a starred problem waits at the desk — is that nothing about tonight's correctness argument will use "majority" as such. It will use only the crowded-club property: every quorum overlaps every other. Majorities are simply the cheapest symmetric way to buy that property. Remember, when we reach the proof, to notice which fact is actually doing the work.

What must the protocol deliver? Three clauses, the same three as last week, with the vocabulary shifted one notch toward practice. A value is *chosen* when the parliament has irrevocably settled on it. Agreement: at most one value is ever chosen — not one per hour, not one per majority; one, full stop, forever. Validity: the chosen value is some motion actually moved — the house cannot invent a by-law nobody proposed. And termination — say it with last week's scars showing — *cannot be guaranteed*; we know this now, we do not pretend otherwise, and the design consequence is stated up front: safety must hold unconditionally, in any weather, under any schedule the adversary picks, while liveness will be purchased separately, with timing assumptions, in part four. This division of the estate is not a compromise we settle for. It is the *correct* engineering response to the Fischer–Lynch–Paterson theorem: since no protocol can promise both under asynchrony, build one whose promises never include the impossible part.

One more foundation stone, and it is tonight's debutante. Why does the field keep saying *majority*? Because of a fact so small it fits in a sentence and so load-bearing it will hold up four episodes: **any two majorities of the same parliament share a member.** Two majorities of our three gentlemen — any two-of-three with any two-of-three — overlap in at least one gentleman; two majorities of five overlap likewise; it is arithmetic, nothing more: two clubs each containing more than half the members cannot be disjoint, for the room is not large enough. The course has been calling this the crowded-club lemma since the plan was drawn, and tonight it finally takes the stage — under the name the literature gives it, which you should carry away beside the image: *quorum intersection*. Feel what it buys: a majority is a quorum with *memory*. Whatever one majority has done, any later majority *contains a witness to it*. No gentleman needs to consult the whole house — the whole house may never be reachable — he needs only a majority, and the intersection guarantees that majorities cannot contradict one another in ignorance. Every protocol tonight, and most of the season, is an exercise in arranging for the right witness to be in the right club at the right time.

### Part Two — The Derivation, Act One: Three Ways to Die

Now we build, and fail, and build. I ask you to play along honestly, sir — at each stage, believe the protocol, as its Tuesday designer believed it.

**Attempt the first: first come, first served.** The obvious parliament: every gentleman accepts the first motion to reach him, and never another; a motion supported by a majority is chosen. Simplicity itself, and it even has the crowded club on its side: two different motions cannot both collect majorities, because the shared member of the two clubs would have had to accept both, and the rule forbids him a second acceptance. Safety, proven, in one breath. Run it. Bingo moves free Thursday delivery and writes to the house. Tuppy, concurrently — merely elsewhere, as we learned to say — moves a sixpence surcharge instead. And Gussie, in a spirit of independent inquiry, moves that the shop stock tea. The Post shuffles honestly; the letters land; and the votes fall one, one, and one — Bingo accepted his own motion first, Tuppy his, Gussie his. No majority anywhere. And now attend to the corner we are in: every gentleman has spent his single acceptance. No future letter can move any of them. The parliament is not deadlocked by crash or by lost mail — every machine is healthy, every letter arrived — it has voted itself into a wall, permanently, by the ordinary operation of its own rule. First-come-first-served is safe the way a sealed room is burglar-proof.

The lesson: acceptors must be able to change their minds, or split votes end the republic. Very well —

**Attempt the second: latest word wins.** Very well, says the Tuesday designer, rubbing out one line: let a gentleman accept every motion that arrives, each superseding the last, and let chosen mean a majority currently agrees. Stage it, briefly, because the failure deserves to be seen rather than asserted. Bingo's free-delivery letters land at Bingo and Gussie; Bertie, auditing the house at that moment, finds two ledgers of three reading free delivery — a majority; he notes the by-law settled and instructs his tailor accordingly. But Tuppy's surcharge letters were merely dawdling, clause one of the charter, and presently they land — at Gussie and at Bingo both, superseding. A second learner — Bertie's aunt, let us say, auditing an hour later with identical diligence — finds a majority for the surcharge and notes the by-law settled the other way. Two learners, two audits, two verdicts, each impeccable at its instant, and observe that no future audit is safe either, for there is no moment after which the mails are known to be empty. "Currently agrees" is a fiction in a world of letters — you will recognize the ghost of episode two, sir: there is no *the* current state, only states along cuts. Choice must be **irrevocable** — that is the entire content of the word — and perpetual mind-changing is irrevocability's opposite. We need something between one acceptance forever and acceptance without commitment: mind-changing that is *ordered*, where the house can tell an old thought from a new one and never lets the old displace the new.

**Attempt the second and a half — the instinct every operator has next: appoint a chairman.** Why suffer rival motions at all? Let the house agree that Bingo, and only Bingo, proposes; everyone accepts whatever the chair moves; done. And indeed, sir, while Bingo stands healthy and reachable, this works magnificently — a fact we shall exploit before the night is out. But test it against the terrain. The chair goes silent. Crashed, or in the bath? Last week proved the house cannot know. Wait forever, and the parliament has traded its fault tolerance for etiquette — one nap and the republic halts. Appoint a successor, then — Tuppy takes the chair after a decent timeout. But the timeout is a verdict without a body: Bingo may be alive, his motions still crawling through the Post, and now *two* gentlemen believe themselves chairman, each proposing with full authority — which is exactly the rival-motions problem we hired the chairman to abolish, returned wearing a sash. Leadership, sir, does not *solve* agreement; leadership *presupposes* it — agreement on who leads, and agreement on what the old regime did before it fell, neither of which the sash provides. The chairman is a fine idea we are not entitled to yet. To earn him, the house needs machinery that stays safe *while the chairmanship is confused* — machinery indifferent to how many gentlemen currently believe themselves in charge. Hold the thought; it returns in part four with the price tag attached.

**Attempt the third: ballots.** Here enters the object around which everything tonight will turn. Number the attempts. A gentleman wishing to move a motion first takes a **ballot number** — from a supply arranged so no two proposers ever share one; give Bingo the odd numbers and Tuppy the evens and the arrangement is done. The rule of the house becomes: a gentleman accepts the motion of ballot number n unless he has already dealt with a higher-numbered ballot; higher ballots supersede lower ones, never the reverse. A motion is chosen when a majority accepts it *at the same ballot number*. Old thoughts now lose to new thoughts by rule, so the split-vote wall of attempt one falls: whoever tries again at a higher ballot can gather the house afresh. And observe — you heard this coming, sir, at the close of episode two — what a ballot number is: a Lamport clock in parade uniform. A counter that only rises, carried on letters, whose entire purpose is to let a recipient pronounce the word *stale*. I told you the payroll was current.

So run attempt three, and watch it die the interesting death — the one that teaches the real lesson of the evening. Bingo takes ballot number one, moves free delivery, and the Post is kind: Bingo, Tuppy, and Gussie all accept ballot number one, free delivery. A majority — indeed the whole house — at one ballot. **Chosen.** Irrevocably, by our own definition; Bertie is informed; perhaps the Thursday circulars are printed. Meanwhile Tuppy — who, let us say, was slow to hear the outcome; his confirmation letters dawdled; as far as Tuppy knows his colleagues never voted — grows impatient in precisely the way last week's episode licensed him to: silence is not evidence, but one must act regardless. Tuppy takes ballot number two and moves his surcharge. The letters land. And every gentleman, obeying the one rule of the house — higher ballots supersede — accepts ballot number two, the surcharge. Now the ledgers show a majority at ballot number two for the surcharge; any learner arriving now sees the surcharge chosen. The free delivery was chosen, sir — and then it was *unchosen*. The circulars are wrong; Bertie's Thursday is a lie; agreement is dead by overwrite. And nobody misbehaved: Tuppy followed the protocol to the letter. The protocol simply permits a gentleman with a fresh ballot to propose *whatever he pleases*, in perfect ignorance of a decision already taken — and ballots, which order thoughts, do nothing to inform them.

There is the true lesson, and I want it in capitals before we repair anything: **a new ballot must not be free.** The right to propose at ballot number two must come with an obligation — to *learn*, first, what the house may already have done, and to be bound by it. Choice must not merely be irrevocable in the ledgers; it must be irrevocable *against all future ballots*. Which sets our repair problem precisely: arrange matters so that any value chosen at any ballot is the only value any higher ballot can possibly propose. Futures may ratify the past. They may never contradict it.

### Part Three — The Derivation, Act Two: The Synod Stands

The repair comes in two rules, and the second is the deepest thing tonight — the designated set piece, with the wonder budget standing by.

**Repair the first: the promise.** If a new ballot must learn the past before acting, the past must hold still while being learned — you will recognize the shape of this requirement from a certain photograph two weeks ago. So we split a ballot's life into two phases. Phase one, the *prepare*: the proposer of ballot number n writes to the house — not yet moving any motion, merely announcing the ballot — "prepare, ballot number n." A gentleman receiving this, provided he has not already dealt with a higher ballot, replies with two things. First, a **promise**: *I shall entertain nothing below ballot number n from this moment* — and he writes the promise in his ledger before his reply leaves the desk, amnesia being forbidden. Second, a **confession**: the highest-numbered motion he has ever *accepted*, if any — ballot number and value both — so the proposer learns the past from the very gentlemen who constitute it. Two contents, sir, and mark that they face opposite directions: the promise is a vow about the *future*, the confession a disclosure about the *past* — one envelope, two distinct errands, and it will repay you never to fuse them. *Promise* is standard usage; *confession* is the house's word, chosen for the theatre of it — the island paper calls the envelope that carries the pair a *last vote*, and it is under that name you will meet the thing in the literature. When the proposer holds promises from a **majority**, phase one closes and he may proceed. Feel what the promise accomplishes, sir: it freezes the ground under the proposer's feet. The majority that answered him can no longer quietly accept some straggling lower-ballot motion between his reading of the past and his writing of the future — the confession he holds cannot be aged into a lie by mail still in flight. The prepare phase is asking the room's permission while taking the room's deposition, and the promise is what makes the deposition durable.

**Repair the second: adopt the highest.** Phase one closes; the proposer holds a majority's promises and confessions; now what may he move? Here is the rule, and then — because this is the least obvious rule in the protocol, the one that separates everyone who has memorized Paxos from everyone who has understood it — the full ten minutes on why it is not merely sufficient but *forced*. The rule: **among the confessions in hand, find the one bearing the highest ballot number, and propose its value.** Only if every confession in the majority is empty — no one has ever accepted anything — may the proposer move his own motion. His own preference otherwise goes in the drawer, jokes and all.

Why this rule, sir? Why the *highest*? Let me put the alternatives on trial, using the disaster we already own. Return to the moment of Tuppy's ballot number two — replayed now under phase one. Tuppy prepares; Bingo, Tuppy, Gussie promise; and the confessions come back: each says *accepted: ballot number one, free delivery.* If Tuppy may still propose his surcharge — if confessions are merely advisory — we have repaired nothing; so the confessions must bind. Might the rule be "adopt any confessed value," or "the value most gentlemen confess"? Consider what a confession means. The free delivery was *chosen*: a majority accepted it at ballot number one. Tuppy's phase-one majority and that choosing majority are two clubs in one small room — **the crowded club, sir, first blood**: they share at least one member, and that shared gentleman's confession carries the chosen value. It must; he accepted it, and confessions report the highest acceptance, and — hold this thought — nothing *higher* can have displaced it in his ledger yet, because tonight's rule is under construction precisely to ensure higher ballots carry the same value. So the chosen value *will be present* among any majority's confessions. Present — but perhaps not unanimous, and perhaps not even the plurality, because rooms accumulate *debris*, and I want you to see debris manufactured before your eyes, since it is the exact exhibit that convicts the plausible wrong rules.

Run a messier history, five gentlemen now for elbow room — Bingo, Tuppy, Gussie, Barmy, and Oofy. Ballot number one: Bingo moves the surcharge; his accept letters straggle; exactly one — to Oofy — arrives before events overtake it. Oofy's ledger: accepted, ballot number one, the surcharge. One acceptance of five: nothing chosen, a mere fossil of an ambition. Ballot number two: Tuppy prepares. Three gentlemen answer him, and every one of the three confesses an empty ledger — Oofy, who holds the fossil, is not among them; such is the Post. Nothing binds Tuppy, then, and he moves his own motion: free delivery. Now the accepts, one at a time. Tuppy writes it into his ledger; Gussie writes it into his; Barmy writes it into his. Three ledgers of five, all at ballot number two: **chosen.** Free delivery is law, whether or not anyone yet knows it. Now ballot number three: Bingo returns, prepares, and gathers promises from a majority consisting of Bingo, Oofy — and Gussie. The confessions in his hand: Bingo, nothing; Oofy, *ballot number one, the surcharge*; Gussie, *ballot number two, free delivery.* Put the wrong rules on the bench, sir. "Adopt any confessed value" — Bingo may lawfully pick the surcharge, and the chosen by-law is overwritten at ballot number three: dead on arrival. "Adopt the plurality of confessions" — the room shows one vote surcharge, one vote free delivery, a tie resolved by whim: dead the same way, merely ashamed of it. Both rules die because both treat confessions as *opinions to be polled*, when they are *strata to be read*: the fossil at ballot number one is older than the law at ballot number two, and age here is recorded in ballot numbers, not in headcounts. Only one rule reads the strata: the highest-numbered confession — Gussie's, ballot number two, free delivery — is the chosen value. The credential is not popularity. It is the *ballot number* — and here is the induction that closes the trap for every future case at once, the proof strategy performed aloud with the full argument waiting at the desk.

Claim: if a value is chosen at ballot number b, then every ballot numbered higher than b that reaches its proposing phase proposes that same value. Walk the ballots upward in order, sir, and suppose the claim holds for every ballot between b and the one under examination — call the one under examination ballot n. Its proposer holds promises from a majority. That majority intersects the choosing majority of ballot b: some witness in the room accepted the chosen value at b. So the confessions include the chosen value at ballot number b — the witness's promise-ledger may since have recorded acceptances at ballots *between* b and n, but by the very claim we are establishing, walked upward rung by rung, every such intermediate acceptance carries the chosen value again: between b and n, there was nothing else on offer. So consider the highest-numbered confession in the proposer's hands. It is numbered at least b — the witness guarantees that — and every confession numbered b or above carries the chosen value. **The highest-numbered confession is therefore the chosen value**, whatever the debris below it says, however popular the debris. Adopt the highest, and ballot n proposes the chosen value; the claim climbs one more rung; the induction stands. And notice, sir, what the trial of alternatives has revealed: "adopt the highest" is not one good rule among several. Any rule that could ever prefer a lower-numbered confession admits a counterexample built exactly like our disaster — the desk has you construct one — while the highest-numbered confession is the unique position in the room guaranteed to hold the truth. The rule is forced. The scar closes.

And with it, the Synod of Paxos stands complete. Say it once, end to end, in the house style, so you may hear how little of it there suddenly is. Phase one: the proposer of ballot number n writes to the parliament — prepare, ballot number n. Each acceptor, unless already promised to a higher ballot, writes the promise in his ledger and replies: promise — enclosing his highest acceptance, ballot number and value, if ever he made one. Phase two: holding a majority's promises, the proposer moves — accept, ballot number n, and the value the confessions force upon him, his own only if the past is silent. Each acceptor, unless promised meanwhile to a higher ballot, writes the acceptance in his ledger: accepted, ballot number n. And when a majority has accepted at one ballot number, the by-law is chosen — irrevocably, this time in truth, because every future ballot has just been proven a hostage of the past. That is the entire protocol, sir. Two phases, two rules of refusal, one rule of adoption, a ledger, and a crowded room. Everything else ever written about Paxos is performance notes.

And if you keep only one thing from the wiring, sir, keep the three gates — the three places where every decision in this machine is actually taken. The first is the proposer's: he passes from phase one to phase two *only* with a majority of promises in hand; short of a majority he does not proceed at all, but retires and tries again at a higher ballot — and that retirement, repeated, is the whole of the trouble we meet in part four. The other two are each acceptor's, and they differ by a hair that decides everything: he opens his *promise*-gate to any ballot standing strictly *above* his last promise, and his *accept*-gate to any ballot standing *no lower* than it — so a gentleman may always accept the very ballot he has this moment promised, and never one beneath it. Three gates, sir. The entire minuet of Paxos, in every weather the adversary can send, is nothing but gentlemen arriving at those three gates and being let through or turned away.

Let us hear it performed once, clean, at full correspondence, because you have earned a run where nothing goes wrong and every letter now has a reason. The house of three; the past holds our old fossil — Gussie, from some abandoned early skirmish, has in his ledger: accepted, ballot number two, the surcharge; nothing was ever chosen. Bingo, holding the odd numbers and fresh ambitions for free delivery, opens ballot number five. Bingo writes to the house: prepare, ballot number five. Tuppy replies: promise, ballot number five — nothing ever accepted. Gussie replies, in his own good time: promise, ballot number five — and confesses, accepted, ballot number two, the surcharge. Bingo's own ledger answers likewise: promise, nothing accepted. Two promises and his own: a majority; phase one closes. Now the adoption rule reads the room: highest confession, ballot number two, the surcharge. Bingo's free-delivery ambitions go in the drawer — note it well, sir: *nothing was ever chosen*, the fossil was one acceptance in an abandoned ballot, and the rule binds him to it anyway. The rule cannot see whether a confessed value was chosen — that is the whole epistemic predicament — so it must treat any confessed value as *possibly* chosen and defer to the highest. Cautious to the point of superstition, and correct precisely because of it: cheap deference, sir, is the premium on an insurance policy against a catastrophe no one can rule out from inside the room. Bingo writes to the house: accept, ballot number five, the surcharge. Tuppy writes it in his ledger and replies: accepted. Gussie likewise: accepted. A majority has accepted at ballot number five — the surcharge is *chosen*, and Bertie, whose delivery notes have haunted three episodes, may at last be told something that will never afterwards be untrue. And observe the manner of that becoming, sir, for it is the temper of the whole machine: the surcharge turned from motion into law in the silent instant Gussie's acceptance completed the majority — no bell, no herald, no moment any gentleman in the room could point to. The word *chosen* names that fact in the ledgers, never the announcement of it; being chosen and anyone's *knowing* it are different events entirely, and the by-law was law before ever it was told.

I shall spend the wonder budget here, as scheduled, and briefly, on the shape of the thing rather than any one rule. We asked three attempts ago for a parliament that could not disagree with itself, and every failure retaught us the same word: the wall of attempt one, the fog of attempt two, the overwrite of attempt three — each was the past failing to *bind* the future. And the finished machine is nothing but that binding, built twice: promises bind the past against revision from below; adoption binds the future against invention from above. Once chosen, always chosen — not because any gentleman remembers the choosing, sir; no gentleman need ever *know* a choice occurred; the free delivery can be chosen while every member of the house believes the matter still open. The choice is held by the *structure* — lodged in the intersection of clubs, carried forward by witnesses who do not know they are witnesses, adopted by proposers who may believe they are merely being cautious. It is the first machine we have built in this course that is wiser than every one of its parts, and it will not be the last.

### Part Four — The Fine Print

Now the contract's small type, in three clauses, each planted earlier and flowering now.

Clause one: what exactly is guaranteed, and against what. The safety argument you just heard — the induction, the intersection, the adoption — invoked *no clocks, no timeouts, no probabilities, and no luck*. Read it back and check, sir: it is pure bookkeeping about ballots and majorities, valid under any schedule the adversary cares to inflict, any delays, any interleaving of duelling ballots, any pattern of crashes and recoveries the ledgers survive. At most one value is ever chosen, in *any* weather. That is what unconditional safety means, and Paxos delivers it in the asynchronous model where last week's theorem lives. The theorem is not contradicted — attend to what was quietly never promised: that any ballot ever *finishes*.

Clause two, therefore: liveness, purchased separately — and the purchase is compulsory. Stage the failure honestly, with the two gentlemen it belongs to. Bingo prepares ballot number three; the house promises. Before his accept letters land, Tuppy — hearing nothing and growing civil-servant anxious — prepares ballot number four; the house, obedient to its promises, is now closed below four; Bingo's accepts arrive and are politely refused. Bingo, discovering himself superseded, prepares ballot number five; Tuppy's accepts arrive into a house promised to five; refused. Tuppy prepares ballot number six — you perceive the rhythm, sir. Two flawlessly polite gentlemen, each forever asking the room's permission and each thereby cancelling the other's, an infinite minuet of prepares in which no accept ever lands on open ground. Nothing in the protocol forbids it: this is last week's forever-on-the-fence, no longer an abstract adversary construction but a plain operational hazard with names attached — the duelling proposers. Last week I told you the theorem's production shadow was the election storm, term numbers climbing while no term completes; you have now been introduced to the storm's two dancers, and have watched the ballots do the climbing. When your monitoring some night shows a coordination cluster's epoch counter ratcheting upward at a steady, fruitless clip, you will know precisely which minuet is playing, and precisely which nineteen eighty-five theorem is calling the tune. And the escape is exactly the one gate one licenses: let the timing assumptions of the real world elect a *distinguished proposer* — a single gentleman whom the others, for a while, defer to; today, as the casting has it, Bingo has the chair. One chairman, no duel; ballots issue from one desk; phase one need succeed only once in calm weather, and matters proceed. The chair is won by timeout and held by heartbeat — which is to say, the throne episode two promised you is rented from partial synchrony, and last week's weakest-detector result now cashes its cheque with some ceremony: the *minimum* oracle that makes consensus solvable, you will recall, is exactly an eventual-leader service. Not a coincidence, sir — a design specification, discovered by theorists and implemented by every timeout-driven election in your fleet. And the division of labour must be said in one line, because it is the single most quoted moral of tonight: **the leader is a liveness optimization; safety lives in the quorums.** A second chairman arising in confusion — the deposed Bingo wandering back mid-election — threatens nothing but progress: his stale ballots die against promises, by the same machinery that kills any stale ballot. The throne may wobble freely. The ledgers do not.

Clause three: the ledgers themselves. Every load-bearing word tonight has been *written* — the promise recorded before the reply, the acceptance recorded before the acknowledgment — and this is not implementation fussiness; it is the failure model's bill. Our legislators are part-time: they crash and *return*. A gentleman who promises ballot number four, naps, and wakes with an empty head is a gentleman who will cheerfully accept ballot number three — the very acceptance his promise forbade — and with two such nappers the parliament manufactures two chosen values in an afternoon.
